$comment: Size budgets enforced by `node tools/size/measure.mjs --check`, which CI runs on
every pull request. All figures are BYTES of gzip -9 over the empty-Next.js-app
control, on the basis documented in tools/size/README.md.
Budgets are ceilings, not targets. They are set just above the current measured
value so that unnoticed creep fails a build — the failure this file exists to
prevent is the one that already happened: core grew 5.95 KB across three releases
without anyone seeing it. Raising a budget is a deliberate decision that belongs
in the same change as the growth, with a reason, and never as a fix for a red
build.
`targets` are where DEVP-62 wants these to end up. They are recorded here so the
gap is visible next to the ceiling, but they are NOT enforced — a target that
fails every build is noise, not a signal.
`previous` is the most recently published release, measured by this same harness.
It drives the 'change against the previous release' line so slow creep shows up
as a trend rather than only as a threshold breach.
`initial` and `total` now carry different budgets, and the gap between them is
the code loaded on demand: core's integration runner, and — in the React layer —
the custom-theme runtime. Before either was split out the two numbers were
identical, because nothing in either package was ever loaded on demand.
Keeping both is the point: a future change that merely defers more code will show
`initial` falling while `total` holds, and a change that actually removes code
will move both. Budgeting only `initial` would let the package grow without limit
as long as the growth was lazy.
The React layer's `total` budgets were raised by 0.35 KB when the theme runtime
was deferred, and that is the honest reading of the change: a second chunk costs
its own module wrapper, so `total` rises while `initial` falls 0.66 KB. The rise
is the price of the deferral, not unnoticed creep, which is why it is recorded
here in the same change rather than absorbed by headroom.
@cookieyes/nextjs mounting banner + preferences, mirroring the leaderboard's
fair-cookieyes app. Measured 14609 / 17296 — within 5 bytes of the plain-React
fixture, which is the check that @cookieyes/scripts stays out of the client bundle.
The agreed targets, restated on the measured basis: core under 8 KB and the
interface under 16 KB of compressed initial download. Both are currently MET
(core 7120, interface 14604).
These replace the original <2 KB core / <8 KB interface goals, which were set
against figures that turned out to be 2.9x and 1.5x optimistic and are below the
cost of the code that has to render in the initial HTML. The measured floor, with
every optional subsystem deferred and the badge removed, is 5.29 KB core and
12.01 KB interface; the remaining gap to it is held by subsystems whose deferral
would weaken a consent guarantee for under 400 bytes each.
Targets are recorded, not enforced; `budgets` above is what fails a build.
@cookieyes/core@0.5.0 and @cookieyes/react@0.6.1 as published on npm, installed
from the registry and measured by this harness. Update on every release.
Every published version, measured by this harness on one machine in one sitting,
so the trend is comparable end to end. Bytes, gzip, initial. This is the
evidence for 'it grew and nobody noticed' — and for the fact that the growth is
spread across three releases rather than caused by one thing.
